narrative:
The model determined that you have a 61.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Placing in the second decile is noticeably lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic consistency in the later stages of your studies. This was the single biggest reason the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Next in importance was your LSAT score. At 37, it sits almost exactly at the average of accepted students and therefore worked in your favor, pulling the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the academic-ranking concerns.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Finishing in the third decile, compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants, added further weight toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the model saw your lower decile placements in both early and later undergraduate years as the dominant signals that you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. 

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake key courses to raise your GPA, aim for a higher class rank if possible, and consider retaking the LSAT to create a clearer upward trend before reapplying.
